consensus_summary: The blind consensus treats the 'great fish' of Jonah primarily as God's appointed instrument of preservation and deliverance, above all a type of Christ's burial and resurrection ('the sign of Jonah,' Matt 12:39-40). A common but distinct alternative stream reads sea-monsters (Leviathan, Rahab, tannin) as chaos powers or hostile empires (Egypt, Babylon) whom God defeats; other alternatives include fish as gathered believers and the extrabiblical ICHTHYS emblem of Christ.
book_summary: The book identifies the fish/great fish/sea-monster as a devouring kingdom that swallows God's people and is compelled to disgorge them, citing Babylon swallowing Israel like a dragon and casting her out (Jer 51:34) and Pharaoh as a whale in the seas (Ezek 32:2), with a cross-reference indicating this reading is carried into the Jonah 'sign of Jonah' material. The book explicitly flags the common rescue-instrument/tomb-type reading as merely 'commonly taught.'
consensus_core_identification: God's appointed rescue-instrument for Jonah, typologically the grave/Sheol from which Christ rose after three days.
book_core_identification: A hostile devouring kingdom/empire that swallows God's people and is forced to give them back.
boundary_disagreement: The book merges Jonah's great fish into the sea-monster-as-empire stream that the consensus deliberately keeps separate (Responses A and B both note these referents 'should not be treated as one uniform symbol'). Cases the consensus assigns to divine providence/resurrection typology (Jonah's fish) are reclassified by the book as instances of imperial swallowing-and-disgorging, alongside Babylon (Jer 51:34) and Pharaoh (Ezek 32:2).
material_contradiction: The consensus core makes the fish a benevolent instrument appointed by God for Jonah's preservation and a figure of the tomb from which Christ rose; the book makes it a hostile, devouring political power acting as an adversary that must be forced to release its prey. A divinely appointed rescue vehicle and a God-opposing devouring kingdom cannot both be the central identification of the same symbol in the same sense; the book's own 'commonly taught' note signals deliberate replacement of the standard identification.
rationale: The book's identification is not novel in the abstract—the empire/sea-monster reading appears in the consensus as a common alternative (Ezek 29:3; 32:2; Isa 51:9), and Response B even lists 'Jonah's fish represents a particular political empire' as a minority reading. But the classification turns on the core: the book displaces the consensus primary (rescue-instrument/resurrection-type) and installs the hostile-kingdom reading as the governing meaning of the whole term, including (per the ch. 4 cross-reference) Jonah's fish. That is replacement of the central referent's character, not mere boundary adjustment, so DIVERGENT with CONTRADICTS at the core and PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION at the extension, since some consensus cases (Ezekiel's monster, chaoskampf texts) are retained while Jonah's fish is reassigned.
strongest_objection: One could argue for REFINED or even MATCH-with-an-alternative: the devouring-kingdom reading is explicitly listed in the consensus (sea-monsters as hostile empires such as Egypt and Babylon, citing the very verse Ezek 32:2 the book prints), and Response B anticipates the Jonah-as-empire extension as a minority view. On that view the book merely promotes a recognized alternative to primacy rather than contradicting consensus. This objection is weakened because the instructions center the comparison on the consensus's core identification (rescue-instrument/tomb type), which the book's core cannot coexist with; also, the printed citations support kingdoms-as-swallowing-monsters (Jer 51:34's 'swallowed me up... cast me out') but do not themselves establish the forced-restoration mechanism (that is Jer 51:44, uncited) or the application to Jonah's fish, keeping citation support partial.
